issues.legal_issue: A title suit challenging registered conveyances is not barred by limitation where the property remained in a third party’s exclusive possession until that person’s death before the suit was filed.
material_facts: The suit challenged registered conveyances made in favour of the defendants’ predecessor in title.
The lower courts had concurrently found that a sub-tenant exclusively possessed the property until his death in 1956.
issues.conclusion: The suit was within limitation, and the High Court’s finding on that issue was affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court affirmed the High Court’s limitation finding on the basis of the concurrent finding that a third party had exclusive possession until his death. The judgment does not identify a separate limitation provision as the basis for that conclusion.

predicates.title_suit_challenging_registered_convey: A person brought a title suit challenging registered conveyances of the property.
predicates.third_party_exclusively_possessed_proper: A third party exclusively possessed the property until that person died.
predicates.suit_filed_after_possession_ended: The suit was filed after the third party’s exclusive possession had ended.

issues.definition: When a title suit challenging registered conveyances is filed after a third party’s exclusive possession has ended with that person’s death, the suit is not barred by limitation.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings that conveyances were forged and that a will was genuine may be affirmed where the findings have evidentiary support beyond expert opinion alone.
material_facts: The trial and first appellate courts found the conveyances forged.
The findings relied on handwriting-expert evidence and witness testimony that the alleged transferor was living elsewhere when the conveyances were executed.
The lower courts also found the will genuine, and the High Court treated that determination as a concurrent finding of fact.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s finding on the evidentiary challenge was affirmed, as were the concurrent factual findings concerning the forged conveyances and the genuineness of the will.
issues.legal_principle: The Court affirmed the concurrent factual findings because they were supported by expert evidence and witness testimony. It did not state a separate rule or cite an earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.civil_appeal_challenging_concurrent_fact: A civil appeal challenged factual findings reached concurrently by the lower courts.
predicates.findings_supported_by_expert_evidence: The findings were supported by expert evidence.
predicates.findings_supported_by_witness_testimony: The findings were supported by witness testimony about the relevant person’s residence when the documents were executed.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal challenges concurrent factual findings supported by expert evidence and witness testimony, those findings are upheld.

issues.legal_issue: Before the relevant amendment, a landholder could not transfer agricultural land by will where the governing succession provisions did not recognize a bequest.
material_facts: The property was agricultural land governed by the applicable land-revenue legislation.
The landholder executed a will before the amendment that added bequests to the permitted modes of devolution.
The landholder died before that amendment came into force.
issues.conclusion: The will could not transfer the landholder’s interest because the unamended law did not recognize transfer by will; the question of entitlement through the alternative inheritance pleading was remitted for fresh consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Under the unamended Sections 164 and 165 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, succession to a Bhumiswami’s rights followed the statutory order, and transfer under Section 165 was otherwise than by will. The 1961 amendment added bequest as a mode of devolution, but the landholder died before it applied. The Court relied on Nahar Hirasingh and Ors. v. Dukalhin and Ors., AIR 1974 MP 141, which held the earlier succession provision valid and applicable despite the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, in light of Article 254(2) of the Constitution and the presidential assent to the land-revenue legislation.

predicates.agricultural_land_title_proceeding_claim: A title proceeding concerning agricultural land claimed the landholder’s interest through a will.
predicates.landholder_died_before_bequest_was_recog: The landholder died before the governing law recognized bequest as a mode of devolution.
predicates.will_made_before_bequest_was_recognized: The will was made before the governing law recognized bequest as a mode of devolution.

issues.definition: In an agricultural-land title proceeding, if the landholder died and the will was made before the law recognized bequest, the will does not transfer the landholder’s interest.

issues.legal_issue: A pleading amendment adding an alternative inheritance basis should not be rejected merely because it changes the suit’s basis or is sought at the appellate stage, absent bad faith or irremediable prejudice.
material_facts: The original suit relied on a will as the basis for claiming title.
The plaintiffs sought to amend the plaint to add an alternative claim based on inheritance and to plead the interests of additional plaintiffs.
The High Court rejected the amendment as changing the basis of a long-pending suit and did not consider the amended pleading when deciding the succession issue.
The Supreme Court held that the amendment sought in the original plaint should have been allowed.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should have allowed the amendment. Its finding on the succession issue was set aside, and that issue was remitted for fresh decision taking the amended claim into account.
issues.legal_principle: Procedural rules are handmaids to the administration of justice, and just relief should not be denied for procedural error unless the applicant acted mala fide or caused injury that cannot be compensated by costs. In Jai Jai Ram Manohar Lal v. National Building Material Supply, Gurgaon, AIR 1969 SC 1267, the Court held that amendment powers serve the needs of justice and are not governed by narrow technical limitations. In Pandit Ishwardas v. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1979 SC 551, the Court held that an appellate court may permit a new plea by amendment, subject to the usual principles; delay and the reason for not seeking amendment earlier are relevant, but the absence of material already before the court is not an absolute bar.

predicates.appellate_proceeding_reviewing_rejection: An appellate proceeding reviewed a decision rejecting an application to amend pleadings.
predicates.party_sought_alternative_inheritance_cla: A party sought to add an alternative claim based on inheritance.
predicates.amendment_rejected_as_changing_suit_basi: The amendment was rejected on the ground that it would change the basis of the suit.

issues.definition: When an appellate court reviews rejection of an amendment adding an alternative inheritance claim and the amendment was rejected as changing the suit’s basis, the amendment should be allowed and the affected issue reconsidered.
